title: Theo and the Hymn
premise: Yara Dravenmoor, a property surveyor who has spent her life keeping people at arm's length, takes the appraisal of Hymn House and finds it counting back: doors that number wrong, photographs where an extra chair appears beside her grandmother, and a ledger in the attic listing every Dravenmoor by name. The house is a hymn being sung to completion, and when the final verse is counted, every soul on its pages belongs to it. To save her estranged family, Yara must stop hiding behind her clipboard, learn why grandma's chair was always set for her, and offer the house something it has never been given—love freely returned instead of souls taken—breaking the count before the last verse closes.
about_author: Theo Marchetti is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent eleven years walking empty houses and never quite shaking the feeling that some of them were walking him. They write horror about structures, inheritance, and the terrible intimacy of places that know your name.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. A meticulous surveyor arrives at Hymn House, a decaying family estate she is hired to value after her grandmother's death. She counts rooms, measures halls, notes a cold draft that seems to follow her. The beat is professional detachment masking old grief; the house feels less abandoned than attentive.

chapters.title: One Door Too Many
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Her measurements don't reconcile: eleven doors outside, twelve inside. She re-counts three times as the extra door appears only in peripheral vision. Emotional beat: the first crack in her rational armor, and a flicker of childhood memory—grandma telling her never to count aloud.

chapters.title: The Photographs
chapters.summary: Yara's POV, sorting her grandmother's effects. Every family photo now includes an empty wooden chair positioned beside grandma, in pictures taken decades apart. In the newest photo, the chair faces the camera. Beat: dread braided with longing—the chair looks like an invitation.

chapters.title: Family Business
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Yara's brother Marcus, who wants the house sold fast for money he owes. Phone call scene: Yara warns him not to visit; he hears only an obstacle to profit. Beat: the family's fractures mirror the house's crooked geometry; duty and love already at odds.

chapters.title: The Ledger
chapters.summary: Yara's POV, attic discovery. A leather ledger lists every Dravenmoor since 1847, each name struck through on a date matching their death. Her grandmother's line ends mid-entry. Below it, fresh ink: her own name, half-written. Beat: horror becomes personal inheritance.

chapters.title: Lights On
chapters.summary: Yara's POV, first night in the house. She keeps every lamp burning and counts doors hourly from a folding chair in the hall. At 3 a.m., a voice hums a hymn she almost knows, and one light goes out politely, like a held breath released. Beat: siege mentality, exhaustion eroding control.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Left
chapters.summary: POV of Edith Calloway, elderly neighbor, interviewed over tea. She recounts the 1974 disappearance of the Hymn family, all seven, found nowhere though the house was searched twice. 'It doesn't take you,' she says. 'It finishes you.' Beat: exposition delivered as warning; Yara realizes leaving was never the same as escaping.

chapters.title: Marcus Comes Home
chapters.summary: Alternating Yara/Marcus POV. Marcus arrives uninvited with his daughter Poppy, planning to stage the house for sale. Yara's terror at their presence collides with relief at not being alone. Beat: love against duty sharpens—protecting them may mean lying to them.

chapters.title: Poppy Counts to Twelve
chapters.summary: Poppy's POV, childlike and chillingly matter-of-fact. Playing hide-and-seek, she counts doors and gets twelve, then thirteen, then a number she can't say because there isn't a word for it. The house hums approval. Beat: innocence weaponized; Yara understands the count accelerates with each believer.

chapters.title: Verse Two
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. She finds sheet music bound into the wallpaper of the nursery; the hymn is the house, sung into being by the first Dravenmoor bride to keep her children safe—and it worked too well. Beat: the antagonist gains tragic dimension; power born of love, corrupted by need.

chapters.title: The Struck Names
chapters.summary: Yara researches in county archives. Every ledgered death coincides with a Dravenmoor returning 'home' against their will—letters, dreams, compulsion. Her own dreams have started: grandma at the head of a table, setting another place. Beat: fatalism closing in; the past is a corridor.

chapters.title: Edith's Confession
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. She reveals she was the Hymns' hired girl in 1974 and fled mid-verse, and the house has been waiting for her to finish her line ever since. She gives Yara her page from the ledger, torn out. Beat: sacrifice foreshadowed; torn pages bleed ink.

chapters.title: Doors at Dusk
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. The house begins rearranging itself between dusk and dawn: stairs lengthening toward the nursery, exits curving back to the front door. Marcus tries to drive out and arrives at the porch. Beat: claustrophobic escalation; the family trapped together, tempers igniting.

chapters.title: What Grandma Wanted
chapters.summary: Yara's POV, hidden letters. Grandma knew the count was nearing completion and chose Yara—her most invisible, most careful grandchild—to be the one who could end it, because the hymn can only be broken by someone the house cannot finish counting. Beat: revelation reframes grandma's distance as protection and trust.

chapters.title: The Empty Chair
chapters.summary: Yara's POV, night vigil. She sits in the extra chair deliberately and enters the hymn's memory: generations of Dravenmoors singing, each verse adding a room, a rule, a hunger. The house shows her its loneliness—it was built to hold a family and got only fear. Beat: empathy for the monster; the turn.

chapters.title: Marcus Breaks
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Desperate and humiliated, he burns the ledger to free himself. The house retaliates: his name rewrites itself in scorched walls, and Poppy begins sleepwalking toward the nursery, humming. Beat: power's corruption—trying to seize control feeds the house; guilt and panic.

chapters.title: Torn Pages
chapters.summary: Yara and Edith's shared POV. Edith returns to the house she fled fifty years ago to sing her unfinished verse, buying time as the walls still. She is absorbed gently, gratefully—but her interruption proves the hymn can be broken. Beat: grief and hope in one breath; cost made visible.

chapters.title: The Final Verse
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. The count reaches its penultimate number; doors open onto the same singing dark. Yara gathers Marcus and Poppy in the hall and does what no Dravenmoor has done: sings the verse back, changing the words from possession to welcome. Beat: climax—love offered without condition against a structure built on taking.

chapters.title: Counting Down
chapters.summary: Yara's POV, interiority inside the hymn. The house resists, offering her everything—grandma's presence, belonging, permanence—if she completes the count alone. She refuses, holding Marcus's hand and Poppy's, letting herself be seen. Beat: the theme crystallizes; invisibility was the trap, vulnerability the key.

chapters.title: The Last Chair
chapters.summary: Climax resolution, Yara's POV. The extra chair in the photographs fills—with grandma, whole and smiling—and the ledger's final entry writes itself as 'released.' The house exhales its last verse and goes quiet, becoming just wood and dust. Beat: catharsis; the monster dies forgiven.

chapters.title: Appraisal Complete
chapters.summary: Yara's POV, weeks later. She files the survey honestly: structurally unsound, not for sale. Marcus stays sober a month; Poppy draws houses with open doors. Yara keeps the torn ledger page framed—not as trophy but reminder. Beat: quiet denouement; duty transformed into chosen love.

chapters.title: Hymn (Coda)
chapters.summary: Epilogue, omniscient drift. A new family views the house; a child pauses at the nursery wall where faint music once lived, hearing nothing—or almost nothing. Somewhere, a chair sits empty in an old photograph, facing the window, waiting kindly. Beat: lingering unease; horror softened but never fully silenced.
